Voice cloning launches in seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices. Amazon Polly is a managed service that turns text into natural-sounding speech. With voice cloning, you can give your brand one recognizable voice across IVR and contact centers, voice agents, mobile apps, advertising, and connected devices. You can also create multiple voices for content creation use cases such as audiobooks, e-learning, podcasts, videos, and game characters. Amazon Polly does not retain a copy of your voice recordings once the voice is created and doesn't use them to train Polly models. Voice cloning is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). Voice cloning is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. To request access, contact your AWS account team or apply here . Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and you pay for the speech you synthesize, on a pay-as-you-go basis. For more details, see the Amazon Polly documentation , and Amazon Polly Pricing page. For speech AI use cases, you can build with Amazon Polly, including voice cloning. Check out the Amazon Polly GitHub repo .

items.title: AWS Network Firewall launches explicit proxy functionality and NAT Gateway association
items.description: You can now associate AWS Network Firewall with NAT Gateway and use it both as an explicit proxy and a transparent firewall with native network address translation. You can use this capability with existing Network Firewall features to filter traffic to and from your applications and prevent data exfiltration and malware injection. AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC. Customers use it to filter their traffic and secure AWS resources. With this launch, you can configure Network Firewall with native NAT Gateway association and use it for both explicit proxy and routed filtering functionalities. Both these functionalities are governed by a single security policy that you maintain centrally. This capability works with existing Network Firewall features including managed rule groups from Amazon or Marketplace, active threat defense, Geo-IP filtering, URL and domain category filtering, container attribute-based rules for Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS, etc. You can access Network Firewall from any VPC in your environment, even the ones with overlapping IP CIDR space, using VPC endpoints. Your traffic reaches the firewall via the VPC endpoint and the filtered traffic exits directly from the NAT Gateway using its IP address. This capability is available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Frankfurt), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Thailand), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Europe (Spain). To learn more about Network Firewall proxy and NAT Gateway association, please visit Network Firewall documentation and pricing page

items.title: Amazon Inspector Code Security adds GitHub Enterprise Server and private connectivity
items.description: Amazon Inspector Code Security now supports GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) integration and private network connectivity for GHES and GitLab Self-Managed. Code Security is also launching automatic fix pull requests in public preview. Organizations that host GHES or GitLab Self-Managed in private networks can now connect through Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) configurations or AWS CodeConnections, so they can scan repositories without opening their firewalls to the entire AWS IP address range. Amazon Inspector Code Security scans first-party application source code, third-party dependencies, and Infrastructure as Code for vulnerabilities in repositories on GitHub, GHES, and GitLab Self-Managed. With automatic fix pull requests, Amazon Inspector turns its suggested fix into a pull request that developers review and choose whether to merge, instead of applying the fix by hand. It opens pull requests only for high-confidence fixes to static application security testing (SAST) findings at or above a severity you set. These features are available in all 10 AWS Regions where Amazon Inspector Code Security is available: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Singapore). To learn more, see the Amazon Inspector User Guide and the Amazon Inspector product page .

items.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity adds private certificate authority support
items.description: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now supports private certificate authorities (CAs) for custom OAuth 2.0 credential providers. If you already connect your agents to identity providers (IdPs) hosted in your VPC, you can now configure those connections to trust certificates issued by your own CA - including AWS Private CA, enterprise CAs, and self-signed root CAs. AgentCore Identity has supported private IdP connectivity through Amazon VPC Lattice, but until now the IdP still had to present a publicly trusted TLS certificate over that private connection. With private CA support, you store your CA certificate in AWS Secrets Manager or Amazon S3 and reference it from your credential provider configuration. AgentCore Identity uses it to verify the IdP's server certificate directly, removing the need for a publicly trusted certificate or additional infrastructure on the private network path. You can rotate the CA certificate without downtime by combining the current and new certificates in a single PEM file, and remove private CA trust by updating the credential provider without the certificate reference. Private CA support for AgentCore Identity is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Identity supports private IdP connectivity. To get started, see Connect to private identity providers in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To learn more, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page .

items.title: AWS Partner Central Agents now generate Value Realization Plans
items.description: Today, AWS announces that AWS Partner Central Agents can now generate Value Realization Plans (VRPs) for the Business Value Realization (BVR) motion in AWS Partner Central . The VRP is the plan of record for a BVR engagement. The agentic experience generates a VRP that includes the customer's business goals; plan for adoption, change management, and governance; and baseline key performance indicators (KPIs) for Partners to review and finalize. AWS Partner Central launched the BVR motion on June 16, 2026, to help Partners drive business outcomes for their customers by structuring AWS service adoption into defined stages, with funding tied to demonstrated value. With this launch, Partners in the BVR motion no longer start a VRP from a blank page. The agents recommend KPIs, ramp targets, and baseline measurements based on nomination data, opportunity context, and service benchmarks. They also flag gaps before submission, such as a lack of customer sponsorship, and identify next steps. Partners start from a complete draft and refine it with their customer. BVR is available in AWS Partner Central for consulting, system integrator, and managed services partners with Advanced or Premier tier status and a qualifying domain competency. This capability is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. To get started, partners sign in to AWS Partner Central and choose Funding benefits, Business Value Realization. After AWS approves a nomination, partners ask AWS Partner Central Agents, "Help me draft a Value Realization Plan for my BVR engagement." To learn more, see Business Value Realization .

items.title: AWS Network Load Balancer now supports mutual TLS authentication
items.description: AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB) now supports mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication for clients that present X.509 certificates. Until now, customers who needed mTLS with NLB built their own solutions or ran third-party proxies to authenticate clients. With this launch, NLB verifies client certificates on its TLS listeners, so only trusted clients can reach your targets. You can offload the compute-intensive processing required for mTLS authentication to NLB, without adding certificate logic to your backend applications. Mutual TLS is commonly used to secure communication between IoT devices, APIs, and microservices, and in regulated environments where both sides must prove their identity. To use mTLS, create a trust store with a certificate authority (CA) certificate bundle from a CA of your choice or AWS Private Certificate Authority, and attach it to a new or existing NLB TLS listener. To block certificates you no longer trust, add one or more certificate revocation lists (CRLs) to the trust store. To admit only specific clients, add client certificate filters that match the Common Name, Organizational Unit, or the DNS name or URI in the Subject Alternative Name, such as a SPIFFE ID. You can set up mTLS with the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or APIs. Mutual TLS for NLB is available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where NLB is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Blog and the NLB User Guide.

items.title: Amazon Cognito now supports dynamic client registration
items.description: Amazon Cognito now supports OAuth dynamic client registration (DCR, RFC 7591). Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices in minutes. With DCR support, Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients and AI agents can register themselves at runtime. Previously, you had to create an application client in advance for each AI client before it could connect to an MCP server that uses Cognito for authorization. With DCR, Cognito advertises a registration endpoint in its OAuth authorization server metadata. MCP clients that support dynamic client registration discover the endpoint, register to receive a client ID, and then sign users in. You control who can register: either require registration requests to present an access token with a registration scope, or turn on open registration so that any client can register. Dynamically registered clients appear with your other app clients with a client ID prefix and a client type you can filter on, so you can manage them with the same console and APIs. DCR is available on the Essentials and Plus feature plans in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see Dynamic client registration in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

items.title: Amazon S3 Tables now support promoting replicas to writable tables
items.description: Amazon S3 Tables replication now lets you make a read-only replica of your Apache Iceberg table a standalone, writable table with a single API call. S3 Tables replication keeps read-only replica tables in sync with your source tables across table buckets, AWS Regions, and accounts. Instead of copying a replica into a new table, you can promote it in place to move writes to another Region. When you disassociate a replica from replication, the standalone table keeps its namespace and table name, so your queries and pipeline code carry over when you point your applications at it. The promoted table then works like an S3 table you created, and you can use it as a source for new replicas. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables replication is supported. You can use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or S3 Tables API. For pricing details, visit the Amazon S3 pricing page . To learn more, see the S3 Tables overview page and documentation .

items.title: AWS AppConfig launches support for managing native AI model and AI prompt configuration
items.description: Today, AWS AppConfig introduces two new configuration profile types to help you manage the settings for your generative AI applications: AI model invocation configurations, and AI prompt configurations. You can now change model settings and prompts while your application is running, without redeploying code. These updates use AWS AppConfig's safe deployment practices, including gradual rollouts and automatic rollback. This can allow you to move faster and safer, and avoid unexpected behaviors and tokenomics results with rapidly evolving AI solutions. AI model invocation configurations store the settings your application uses to call an AI model. These include the model identifier, inference parameters such as temperature and maximum tokens, and messages such as system prompts and example conversation turns. Provider-specific options are managed in custom parameters, so the same schema works across AI providers. Similarly, AI prompt configurations store prompts as separately versioned artifacts. You can update  and optimize a prompt on its own,without changing the model configuration, and reuse it across multiple applications. This allows for powerful prompt engineering. You can roll out a change to these gradually, for example to 10%, then 20%, then 30% of your traffic. Along the way, you can measure the change's effect on operational metrics, customer experience, and token usage. If an alarm in Amazon CloudWatch, Datadog, New Relic, or another observability solution goes off during the rollout, AWS AppConfig can automatically roll the change back to the previous state.

items.title: AWS CloudFormation StackSets adds progress visibility to simplify tracking deployments at scale
items.description: AWS CloudFormation StackSets now shows stage-by-stage progress for deployments across accounts and AWS Regions, whether you target tens of accounts or thousands. You can follow each deployment as it progresses and take action when needed, without waiting for it to finish. StackSets lets you consistently apply the same infrastructure or application components, such as networking and security settings, across many accounts and Regions in one operation. With this launch, you can see how many stack instances are deployed, how many remain, and which ones need attention. This gives you confidence that a rollout is on track at every stage. Stage-level progress gives you a clear, detailed view of where each deployment stands. Previously, a StackSets deployment showed an overall status while it ran. Now, StackSets also reports progress for two stages. The first is role provisioning, which prepares access in each target account of a service-managed stack set. The second is stack deployment, which deploys your template as a stack instance in each account and Region. For example, in a deployment to 2,000 accounts in 3 Regions, you can see that role provisioning is complete and stack deployment has reached 40 percent, with 2,400 stack instances completed and 3,600 pending. Progress for each Region and the result of each stage remain available after the deployment completes. To get started, open the Progress view for a stack set operation in the CloudFormation console, or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. Existing integrations continue to work without changes. Visit the StackSets documentation to learn more. Deployment progress is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where CloudFormation StackSets is supported. Refer to the AWS Region table for service availability details.

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Memory is now generally available
items.description: Today, AWS announced the general availability of Amazon OpenSearch Memory, a new serverless capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service for adding persistent memory to AI agents. OpenSearch Memory stores agent interactions as searchable events, derives useful memories, and retrieves relevant context across sessions, so agents can recall prior decisions, earlier interactions, and user preferences without replaying the full conversation history to the model. Customers can give agents long-term memory without provisioning infrastructure or building separate extraction, indexing, consolidation, and retrieval systems. OpenSearch Memory stores the original events verbatim, makes them searchable within seconds, and asynchronously derives structured memories. It manages the full memory lifecycle, including extraction, embedding, indexing, consolidation (adding, updating, or skipping memories as new information arrives), and retrieval using keyword, semantic, and hybrid search. Customers control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) for each memory store, with actor and session scoping, and can set expiration periods for events and memories. Because it is serverless, there are no clusters to provision, instance types to choose, or indexes to create, and capacity for extraction and search scales automatically. Amazon OpenSearch Memory is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Regions. For pricing details about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, visit the pricing page . To learn more about Amazon OpenSearch Memory, see the technical documentation and launch blog . You can get started by visiting the technical launch blog that details how to add persistent memory to your agents with Amazon OpenSearch Memory.

items.title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for AWS Glue ETL
items.description: AWS Glue ETL now offers the Apache Spark Optimization Agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations within minutes. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and reasoning behind each suggestion. You can use the agent on any completed job run from the AWS Glue console, or from your own tools through the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server. The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen goal and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. When cost and performance trade off, the agent improves the metric you chose while keeping any regression of the other within defined limits. The engine also checks best practices such as platform-level improvements like upgrading to a newer AWS Glue version or using AWS Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the area it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. All access is authenticated with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and logged in AWS CloudTrail. The Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge for AWS Glue versions 4.0 and later in all Regions where AWS Glue is available, except the AWS GovCloud (US) and China Regions. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR and AWS Glue and the blog post - Introducing the Apache Spark optimization agent for Amazon EMR Serverless and AWS Glue ETL .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports cross-Region inference routing
items.description: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI announces cross-Region inference routing, which helps keep inference applications available when a region runs short of capacity by sending requests to endpoints deployed in other AWS Regions and AWS accounts. Models served on accelerated instances can reach capacity limits in a single Region, and an unhealthy endpoint can lead to throttling and errors for end users. Previously, teams had to build and maintain their own routing, health checks, and retry logic across Regions. With cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, developers create an inference router, register the real-time endpoints, asynchronous endpoints, and inference components they already run, and point their applications at the router. The router prefers endpoints in its own Region, shifts new requests to healthy destinations in other Regions as errors rise, and returns traffic gradually after the local endpoint recovers. Existing endpoints, models, and containers do not change. Endpoint owners stay in control: an endpoint policy determines which routers in other accounts can use an endpoint, and an optional cross-Region traffic cap reserves capacity for the endpoint’s local callers. Each real-time response identifies the endpoint that served the request and the reason, and router metrics in Amazon CloudWatch show where traffic went. Cross-Region inference routing is available for real-time inference in 32 commercial AWS Regions, and for asynchronous inference in 25 Regions. There is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing. Customers pay standard SageMaker AI pricing for the endpoints that serve requests and standard Amazon CloudWatch rates for router metrics. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide and SageMaker AI Deployment page .

items.title: AWS announces ExtendDB 1.0
items.description: Today, Amazon Web Services (AWS) announced version 1.0 of ExtendDB, the first release of the open source Amazon DynamoDB-compatible adapter for production use. ExtendDB is fully compatible with the DynamoDB API and runs on a database backend that you choose, so developers and infrastructure teams can run DynamoDB workloads in on-premises data centers, in private or public clouds, and at the edge without rewriting application code. ExtendDB 1.0 supports four storage backends, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Cassandra, and MongoDB. For local development and continuous integration (CI), the extenddb-dev container image and the @extenddb/dev npm package run a DynamoDB-compatible endpoint over SQLite, so you don’t have to set up an external database. ExtendDB is maintained by AWS, released under the Apache 2.0 license, and developed in the open on GitHub. To learn more, see the ExtendDB project page . To get started or contribute, visit the GitHub repository .

items.title: AWS Transform custom now supports cross-account sharing of transformation definitions
items.description: AWS Transform custom now enables you to share transformation definitions (TDs) and their associated lessons across AWS accounts, organizational units (OUs), or your entire organization in AWS Organizations through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). AWS Transform custom is a capability of AWS Transform that performs transformations across your technology stack, including API and framework upgrades, migrations, and language translations. With this launch, you can share TDs as live resources rather than static copies, so consumers run the owner's latest published version by default while the owner maintains full control. As the TD owner, you select from four managed permissions ranging from execute-only (the default) to permissions that allow consumers to use your lessons, contribute lessons back to you, or download the TD. Lessons flow back to the owner only when the permission allows it and the consumer opts in. This capability is particularly valuable for platform engineering teams and AWS Partners who need to deploy standardized transformations across multiple accounts. A central team can create a TD once and share it organization-wide. This feature is available via the AWS Transform CLI and AWS RAM in US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Canada (Central) Regions. To learn more, visit the AWS Transform User Guide .

items.title: Amazon CloudFront standard logging now supports CMCD and additional log fields
items.description: Amazon CloudFront standard logging now supports additional access log fields that were previously available only in CloudFront real-time logs. You can now include these fields in your standard logs and deliver them to Amazon S3, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, or Amazon Data Firehose, without setting up an additional data stream for real-time logs. The new fields include the IP address of the CloudFront server that handled the request, identifiers that separate traffic on a primary distribution from traffic on a staging distribution, and a media quality confidence score. They also include Common Media Client Data (CMCD) fields, which video players send with each request to report details like bitrate, buffer length, and playback session ID. Streaming teams can use these fields to match playback problems that viewers see with CloudFront delivery data, which makes troubleshooting faster. These fields are available in all CloudFront edge locations, and standard logging pricing applies. To learn more, see Standard logging page in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide .

items.title: Amazon CloudFront Announces WebSocket and gRPC Support for Origin Mutual TLS
items.description: Amazon CloudFront (CF) now supports WebSocket and gRPC traffic to application origins in AWS regions, with mutual TLS authentication between CF and the application origin (origin mTLS). Customers can now use TLS certificates to authenticate requests from CloudFront while setting up WebSocket or gRPC connections to their origins. Origin mTLS protects internet facing applications that need persistent, bidirectional or streaming connections, such as chat platforms, collaborative editing tools or live dashboards from unauthenticated requests. Previously, customers serving WebSocket or gRPC traffic through CloudFront had to use shared secrets or IP allow-lists to identify requests originating from CloudFront. This was operationally complex and did not provide strong authentication. With Origin mTLS, customers can use one TLS based authentication for HTTP, WebSocket and gRPC traffic to an application origin. This works with application origins within AWS such as Application Load Balancer and API Gateway, on-premises origins, and origins hosted outside AWS. There is no additional charge for origin mTLS, and it is available with pay-as-you-go pricing and in the Business and Premium flat-rate pricing plans. To learn more, visit the CloudFront origin mutual TLS documentation .

items.title: AWS Lambda adds support for GPU instances on Lambda Managed Instances
items.description: AWS Lambda now supports GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances using EC2 G-series instances . You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads including AI inference, media processing, 3D rendering, scientific computing, and financial simulations on Lambda without managing GPU drivers, frameworks, or scaling. Lambda runs multiple invocations concurrently in each execution environment and scales responsively based on GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency to keep your GPUs busy and reduce costs. GPU-accelerated functions integrate with the same 200+ AWS event sources as other Event Functions, so you can add GPU compute as another step in your serverless application. Running GPU workloads today requires customers to provision hardware, manage driver and framework dependencies, and build custom scaling and capacity management. With this launch, you can go from code to a running GPU workload in minutes. Lambda provides GPU base images preconfigured with frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, and PyTorch. You can run workloads with large artifacts using container images and NVMe ephemeral storage of up to 32 GB each. To reduce startup time, Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading and streaming artifacts directly from Amazon S3. For resilience, you can select G-series instance types from multiple generations in the allowed instance types for your capacity provider. Lambda provisions instances from the newest generation that meets your function requirements and falls back to older generations when capacity is unavailable. GPU-accelerated Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances and EC2 G-series instances are available. You can configure GPU-accelerated functions using the AWS Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use this feature through coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex by installing the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS . You pay the EC2 On-Demand price (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply) for your instance, plus a 9.75% Lambda management fee and $0.20 per million requests. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda Pricing .

items.title: Amazon RDS for MySQL supports MySQL minor version 8.4.13
items.description: Starting today, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for MySQL supports MySQL minor version 8.4.13, the latest minor released by community MySQL. We recommend upgrading to the newer minor versions to accept fixes for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) in prior versions of MySQL and to benefit from bug fixes, performance improvements, and new functionality added by the MySQL community. Learn more about the enhancements in RDS for MySQL 8.4.13 in the Amazon RDS user guide and MySQL 8.4.13 release notes. You can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable automatic minor version upgrades and use the AWS Organizations Upgrade Rollout Policy to orchestrate upgrades across your instances in phases, validating on lower-priority environments before upgrading your most critical ones. You can perform minor version upgrades in-place or via snapshot restore. Learn more about performing version upgrades in the Amazon RDS User Guide . This release is supported in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for MySQL is available. Amazon RDS for MySQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale MySQL deployments in the cloud. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

items.title: Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery
items.description: Amazon Cognito now supports point-in-time recovery (PITR), so you can restore the user data in a user pool to an earlier time. Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices. Previously, you had to build and maintain your own export and restore process, and restored users received new identifiers and had to reset their passwords. With PITR, you choose a recovery point, preview how many users, groups, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys the recovery will create, update, or delete, and then start or cancel the recovery. Recovered users keep their identifiers, passwords, MFA settings, and passkeys, so they can sign in without resetting their credentials. For example, if a script deletes or modifies users by mistake, you can restore the user data to the moment before it ran. PITR is enabled automatically for user pools on the Essentials and Plus feature plans at no additional charge. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. You can initiate and manage a recovery using the AWS Management Console, the Amazon Cognito API, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. PITR is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available. To learn more, see Point-in-time recovery in the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

items.title: Amazon RDS for MySQL now supports MySQL major version 9.7
items.description: Starting today, Amazon RDS for MySQL supports MySQL major version 9.7, the latest Long-Term Support release from MySQL community. Amazon RDS for MySQL 9.7 launches with community MySQL 9.7.4. This launch introduces support for the Replication Applier Metrics component, JSON Duality Views, and Hypergraph Optimizer.   The Replication Applier Metrics help you diagnose replication lag by adding two Performance Schema tables that report per-channel applier backlog, throughput, and wait statistics, along with each worker's progress on its current transaction. JSON Duality Views let applications read and write the same relational tables as JSON documents. The Hypergraph Optimizer is an opt-in query optimizer that can improve execution plans for complex, multi-join queries. For more details, refer to the MySQL 9.7.4 release notes and the Amazon RDS for MySQL release notes . You can upgrade your database using Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments , in-place upgrade, or restore from a snapshot. Learn more about performing version upgrades in the Amazon RDS User Guide . This release is supported in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for MySQL is available. Learn more about pricing details at Amazon RDS for MySQL pricing . Amazon RDS for MySQL makes it simple to set up, operate, and scale MySQL deployments in the cloud. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console or by using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

items.title: Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes reduces price for large hosts
items.description: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Hybrid Nodes now has lower pricing for large nodes, capping the billed vCPU per node at 32 vCPU, so you are no longer charged for vCPUs above that per node threshold. Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes lets you use your existing on-premises and edge infrastructure as nodes in Amazon EKS clusters. You can now use your largest servers, including those with GPUs, with Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes at lower cost. With this change, the Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes cost of a large server no longer grows with its vCPU count. At the first pricing tier, a 64 vCPU node now costs 50% less than before, and a 256 vCPU node costs 88% less, as both are now billed only for 32 vCPUs. This makes Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes more cost-effective for large bare-metal and GPU servers running compute-intensive workloads, such as AI/ML training and inference, that must stay on-premises for data residency, latency, or regulatory reasons. The pricing change applies automatically to all new hybrid nodes. For the new pricing to take effect for existing hybrid nodes attached to clusters, delete and reattach them. Nodes with 32 vCPUs or fewer are still billed for their actual vCPUs, and existing tiered pricing still applies, so your effective rate falls as monthly usage grows. The new pricing is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes is available. To learn more about getting started and updated pricing details, visit the Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes documentation and Amazon EKS pricing page .

items.title: Amazon CloudFront Functions now supports network calls
items.description: Amazon CloudFront Functions can now make network calls and act on the response during a request. CloudFront Functions runs lightweight JavaScript at CloudFront edge locations to customize requests and responses. Previously, if your logic depended on data from another service, you had to use Lambda@Edge or move that logic to your origin. Now your functions can use real-time data to personalize, authenticate, or route requests at the edge, close to your viewers. With the new cf.fetch() method, your functions can call your API endpoints and use the response to decide how to handle each request. For example, you can check an AI agent's permissions and usage budget so that only authorized requests reach your API or MCP server, or send request signals to a security or fraud detection service to block or challenge bad traffic. With cf.beacon() , you can send analytics events in the background without slowing down viewers, even for content served from cache. Both methods take advantage of the origin settings already on your distribution, including origin access control (OAC), VPC origins, and connection reuse. Network calls are available at all CloudFront edge locations. They cost $0.10 per million calls, on top of CloudFront Functions invocation charges, and are included at no additional cost in the Pro plan and above in CloudFront flat-rate plans. To learn more, see Helper methods for network calls in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide and Amazon CloudFront pricing .

items.title: Amazon RDS now supports fast storage volume initialization
items.description: Amazon RDS now initializes storage volumes faster when you perform a point-in-time restore (PITR), create a read replica, or convert a Single-AZ instance to Multi-AZ. Each of these operations creates storage volumes from a snapshot, and the data blocks are downloaded from Amazon S3 before you can access them. With fast storage volume initialization, you get a fully performant DB instance in a predictable amount of time. Previously, the initialization rate varied with your workload and with which blocks were accessed. As there was no dedicated bandwidth, so you could see increased I/O latency and had no way to tell when an instance would reach full performance. Now, each database instance is initialized at up to 4 TiB per hour, across every gp3 and io2 storage volume attached to the instance. If concurrent initialization across your account exceeds the available bandwidth, the remaining blocks initialize on a best-effort basis, so initialization is never slower than today. Your DB instance stays available and usable while initialization runs. Fast storage volume initialization is enabled by default and no action is required. To follow progress, use the StorageOperationStatus and StorageOperationPercentProgress fields in the Amazon RDS console, the DescribeDBInstances API, the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. This capability is available at no additional cost for RDS for MariaDB, RDS for MySQL, RDS for PostgreSQL, RDS for Db2, RDS for Microsoft SQL Server, and RDS for Oracle, in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, see Amazon RDS storage in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

items.title: AWS Clean Rooms supports writing PySpark job results to intermediate tables
items.description: AWS Clean Rooms now supports intermediate tables for PySpark jobs , offering increased flexibility for organizations running complex, multi-step analytical workflows with their partners. With this launch, customers can write the results of a PySpark job to an intermediate table for reuse in subsequent analyses. For example, a measurement vendor can perform feature engineering with PySpark, then use those results as input into an ML model training job to identify new high-value customers to inform audience targeting and bid optimization for their campaigns.   AWS Clean Rooms helps companies and their partners easily analyze and collaborate on their collective datasets without revealing or copying one another’s underlying data. For more information about the AWS Regions where AWS Clean Rooms is available, see the AWS Regions table. To learn more about collaborating with AWS Clean Rooms, visit AWS Clean Rooms .

items.title: AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes, giving platform teams centralized control over runtime contents and updates
items.description: AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes for Lambda Event Functions (formerly Lambda functions). Customer-managed runtimes are a standalone resource type that fully decouples runtime management from function deployment. Platform teams gain centralized control over the runtime contents, updates, access, and lifecycle, including the ability to push updates to shared components without per-function redeployments. Application teams consume the runtime from their functions in the same way as a Lambda-managed runtime, preserving their familiar developer experience. Many organizations require every function to include approved components, such as SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring tools. Previously, sharing these through Lambda Layers or container images meant redeploying every function to pick up a change. With customer-managed runtimes, platform teams manage these components in a central runtime, packaged as OCI container images in Amazon ECR and compatible with existing Docker and CI/CD tooling. Functions pick up updates automatically as Lambda recycles execution environments, so there's no need to redeploy each function or coordinate rollouts. Updates can be scheduled and staged to match change control policies, with centralized health metrics and rapid rollback. With this launch, the existing custom runtimes feature is renamed "bring your own language." AWS Lambda customer-managed runtimes is now generally available in all commercial AWS Regions. There is no additional charge for customer-managed runtimes; functions are billed at standard Lambda rates and standard Amazon ECR pricing applies to runtime images. To get started, build your runtime as a container image in Amazon ECR, starting from a Lambda base image or from scratch, then create a runtime, a version, and an alias. Application teams reference the runtime alias in their function configuration and keep deploying their code as .zip files. Share runtimes with other accounts or an AWS Organization by using a resource-based policy. You can create and manage customer-managed runtimes using the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, CloudFormation, or AWS CDK. To learn more, see the customer-managed runtimes documentation and launch blog post .

items.title: Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports audit logging
items.description: Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports database-internal audit logging, a fully managed capability that captures SQL statements executed on your cluster. Previously, AWS CloudTrail recorded who connected to a DSQL cluster, but not what they did once inside it. Now, financial institutions and regulated enterprises can meet production compliance requirements by capturing DDL, DML, DCL, and SELECT statements with full statement text, bind parameters, acting principal (both PostgreSQL role and AWS IAM identity), timestamp, table name, and transaction identifier. With audit logging, you can feed SIEM systems directly from Amazon S3, satisfy auditor requirements for change accountability, and reconstruct events after security incidents. Logs are delivered as structured JSON to your S3 bucket via CloudWatch Vended Logs. Configuration requires a single SQL setting-no extension to load and no log-shipping pipeline to build. Audit logging is available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available. Audit logging will incur Aurora DSQL DPU charges, charges for log delivery through CloudWatch Logs, and charges for storing audit records in Amazon S3. For pricing information, see Aurora DSQL pricing . To learn more, see audit logging in the Aurora DSQL User Guide.

items.title: Amazon ElastiCache now supports distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLM inference
items.description: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now offers fully managed distributed KV caching, a new capability that reduces self-hosted large language model (LLM) inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Customers who self-host LLMs pay for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can't hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. GPUs can fetch cached KV state in milliseconds to serve more requests and respond faster. Distributed KV caching runs on cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes in the same Availability Zone as the GPU fleet and connects to GPUs through Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).  Distributed KV caching works with open-weight, fine-tuned, and custom models, whether they use full, sparse, hybrid, or other attention designs. You can add distributed KV caching to the inference engines you already use, including vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, through the LMCache connector with a configuration change. You can also use the open-source KVTrace tool to estimate the cost and latency reductions on your own application traffic before deploying anything, at no charge. Distributed KV caching is available today on ElastiCache for Valkey in 13 AWS Regions across the US, Europe, and Asia Pacific. To get started, create a cluster with cache.i8ge.48xlarge nodes using the AWS CLI  in the same AZ as your GPU fleet and adding the endpoint to your inference engine. To learn more, read the AWS blog for a technical deep dive and performance results, or visit the Amazon ElastiCache documentation . For pricing, see the Amazon ElastiCache pricing page .

items.title: Amazon CloudWatch simplifies network performance monitoring for your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
items.description: Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitoring now allows you to monitor the health of the AWS network paths that your workloads take by using performance monitors. Performance monitors provide near real-time visibility into whether the AWS network is healthy for your workloads, without installing any software. Performance monitors report per-path metrics such as latency, a network impact score that shows network health, and traffic volume across all flows in your VPCs. You simply select the VPCs you want to monitor, and metrics are available within minutes. Using telemetry AWS already collects, with no additional services to enable, performance monitors determine the paths your traffic takes, within and across Availability Zones, across AWS Regions, and to AWS services, for TCP, UDP, and ICMP traffic. They then score each path by comparing it with its own recent history and with all other paths AWS measures at the same time. For example, a path that suddenly degrades, or degrades with many other paths during an AWS network event, scores high. Metrics publish to Amazon CloudWatch for dashboards and alarms, and AWS Organizations integration lets you monitor VPCs across accounts and Regions. Performance monitors complement flow monitors in CloudWatch Network Monitoring. When a checkout application slows down, a performance monitor shows whether the path from the web tier in one Availability Zone to the database in another is degraded. A high network impact score points to the AWS network, so your team can engage AWS Support instead of investigating your application. If the path is healthy, you can focus on your own stack, where flow monitors use software agents on Amazon EC2 and Amazon EKS to find affected connections, such as a payment pod retransmitting to the database. For available AWS Regions, see the Regions list . To learn more, visit the Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitoring documentation .

items.title: AWS Control Tower now supports existing Amazon S3 bucket for log delivery
items.description: AWS Control Tower now lets you use an existing Amazon S3 bucket in your landing zone to store AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail logs. Previously, AWS Control Tower required you to use the Amazon S3 bucket it creates and manages for log storage. Now, customers who want full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure can consolidate centralized logs in an Amazon S3 bucket they already manage. You can use your own Amazon S3 bucket for both AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail, giving you full control of bucket policies, lifecycle rules, and logging infrastructure. You can switch between self-managed and AWS Control Tower managed buckets at any time, and your Amazon S3 buckets are preserved during landing zone updates, resets, and decommissioning. The bucket must be owned by an AWS account in your organization, be located in your AWS Control Tower home Region, and be preconfigured with the bucket policy that AWS Control Tower requires. This feature is supported in landing zone version 4.0 and later and is available in all commercial AWS Regions , the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud where AWS Control Tower is available. To learn more about configuring self-managed Amazon S3 bucket for your AWS Control Tower landing zone, visit the AWS Control Tower documentation .

items.title: AWS IAM account access manager is now even easier to deploy and use
items.description: Deploying and using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) account access manager is now even easier: you can use AWS managed policies to enable and administer it; you can include it in your infrastructure-as-code (IaC) configurations; and its role assignments are integrated in a growing number of third-party identity and entitlement management solutions. Administering workforce access with account access manager requires permissions across several services, including AWS IAM Identity Center, AWS Organizations, AWS KMS, and AWS IAM. Previously, defining administrative access required hand-assembling multi-service IAM policies. The new AWS managed policies enable faster ramp up with broadly scoped job-aligned permissions for: 1/ Full administrator (AWSAccountAccessManagerAdministrator) - used to enable and manage account access manager in the AWS organization management account and to map users/groups to IAM roles; 2/ Entitlement Manager (AWSAccountAccessManagerEntitlementManager) - used to assign and remove user access without the ability to change service configuration; and 3/ ReadOnly (AWSAccountAccessManagerReadOnlyAccess) - used by auditors and compliance reviewers for visibility into user access. Account access manager streamlines assignment of IAM roles to workforce users and groups in IAM Identity Center, bringing together access management flexibility, user awareness, and a single point of federation. You can include account access manager in your IaC configurations managed through Terraform, Pulumi, or AWS CloudFormation. The entitlements that you assign with account access manager are reflected in your identity provider (IdP) and entitlements management system, including those offered by AWS partners Okta, PingIdentity, Cisco Duo, Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai, Lumos, and SailPoint. IAM account access manager is provided at no additional cost and available in all AWS Commercial Regions enabled by default. To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide .

items.title: Amazon Braket adds PAUSED device status
items.description: Amazon Braket now offers a new device status, PAUSED, to give customers clear and actionable information on when they can submit quantum tasks and hybrid jobs and when those tasks and jobs will run. Device status now tells you: ONLINE: The device is accepting quantum tasks and hybrid jobs and is actively processing them during its availability window. (New) PAUSED: The device is accepting quantum tasks and hybrid jobs but isn't processing them right now, because it is outside its availability window, in short-term maintenance, or in a reservation. Tasks and jobs you submit stay QUEUED and run once the device is ONLINE. OFFLINE: The device is unavailable and isn't accepting new quantum tasks or hybrid jobs, for example due to scheduled maintenance, upgrades, or operational issues. RETIRED: The device has been permanently decommissioned and is no longer available on Amazon Braket. When a device is PAUSED, a Status Reason is provided with additional information on why it's paused, when the status began, and an estimated end time if one is available. You can view device status on the Devices page in the Amazon Braket console, or programmatically with the GetDevice and SearchDevices APIs or the Amazon Braket SDK. For example, the GetDevice API will return one of the following status reasons for PAUSED state: OUTSIDE_AVAILABILITY_WINDOW, MAINTENANCE, or RESERVATION. Amazon Braket is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Europe (London), and Europe (Stockholm) AWS Regions. To learn more, see the Amazon Braket Developer Guide .

items.title: AWS HealthOmics now supports Nextflow version 26.10
items.description: AWS HealthOmics now supports Nextflow version 26.10, which adds enhancements such as static typing, pipeline composition, and configurable report directories. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. In Nextflow 26.10, static typing lets workflow developers declare types for parameters, inputs, and outputs, and the nextflow lint command reports type errors before any task is submitted. Pipeline composition lets developers include a statically typed pipeline from their workflow package and call it like a sub-workflow, so validated pipelines can be reused as building blocks. For example, you can include an alignment pipeline and a variant-calling pipeline in one workflow, and each sample moves to variant calling as soon as alignment finishes. Collection parameters can now be loaded directly from CSV, JSON, or YAML sample sheets into record types. Execution reports, timelines, and traces can be written to a directory inside the workflow output, and HealthOmics exports them with the run outputs. You can use Nextflow 26.10 in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Singapore, Seoul, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the Nextflow version release notes documentation.

items.title: AWS Deadline Cloud now supports Amazon EC2 G7 instances in service-managed fleets
items.description: AWS Deadline Cloud now supports Amazon EC2 G7 instances in service-managed fleets. Deadline Cloud is a fully managed service that helps teams run compute-intensive workloads for visual effects, animation, product design, simulation, and gaming. G7 instances give customers more options to scale GPU capacity quickly. You can add G7 instances to your service-managed fleets in sizes from g7.2xlarge to g7.48xlarge, with On-Demand or Spot pricing on Linux or Windows workers. This lets you scale GPU rendering capacity to match your production schedule without managing your own render farm infrastructure. To get started, create or update a service-managed fleet in the Deadline Cloud console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs, and select the RTX PRO 4500 GPU accelerator. G7 instances are available in the US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), and Asia Pacific (Sydney) Regions. To learn more, see Use a GPU accelerator in the AWS Deadline Cloud User Guide .

items.title: AgentCore runtime instances now support privileged mode
items.description: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances now support privileged mode, which lets your agents install system-level software and run nested containers. Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. You turn on privileged mode when you create or update an agent runtime that runs on runtime instances. For example, a coding agent can start its service dependencies, such as Postgres and Redis, as containers and run its integration tests against them. A code-modernization agent can install the compilers and libraries that a migration needs. A session that runs a privileged agent runs only that agent, so elevated privileges stay with one agent on its instance. Agents that don't use privileged mode keep the default standard mode, so existing agents don't change. Standard mode suits most agents. Use privileged mode only if your agent needs to install system-level software or run containers. Privileged mode is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore runtime instances are available. To get started, see the following resources: Configure the privilege mode for runtime instances in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide AgentCore pricing

items.title: Amazon S3 Replication adds exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution
items.description: You can now replicate data in Amazon S3 buckets with fewer replication rules using two new S3 Replication capabilities, exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution. Buckets that many tenants or applications share often need many rules to skip certain data or to match encryption keys in each AWS Region. With these capabilities, customers who manage multi-tenant and shared buckets can replace many replication rules with a single rule. With exclusions, you can replicate an entire bucket while skipping specific prefixes or tagged objects, such as logs or experimental data. With Multi-Region key resolution, S3 Replication encrypts each replica with the matching AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) Multi-Region key in the destination Region, so replicas meet the same encryption requirements as their source objects. For example, a bucket that stores data for hundreds of tenants, each with its own Multi-Region key, can replicate with a single rule, including tenants you add later. Exclusions and Multi-Region key resolution are optional and available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions. To get started, use the AWS SDKs, AWS CLI, S3 API, or S3 console. To learn more, visit the S3 Replication product page and Replicating objects within and across Regions in the S3 User Guide.

items.title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports higher pod density on EKS-orchestrated clusters
items.description: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports higher pod density per node on EKS-orchestrated clusters, allowing you to get more out of every instance. This leaves more room for your applications alongside system DaemonSets for monitoring, logging, and security, and helps increase GPU, CPU and memory utilization on nodes, allowing you to run the same work using fewer instances. As you schedule more pods, the Amazon VPC CNI automatically adds network capacity to the node. Autoscaling with Karpenter also supports the higher pod capacity, so new nodes take on more pods as your cluster scales out. Here are a few examples of workloads that benefit from higher pod density: Model inference - Serve more model replicas or more models from each GPU instance, including on smaller types such as ml.g5 and ml.g6. Interactive development - Host more notebooks, IDEs, and data science environments on each node. GPU partitioning - Use all the Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) slices on instances such as ml.p5en.48xlarge, where each slice runs its own pod. Operators and Controllers - Run operators, controllers, and observability agents on CPU nodes alongside your workloads, without crowding them out. This feature is available for HyperPod EKS-orchestrated clusters in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To get started, update your cluster's IAM permissions, cluster software, and Amazon VPC CNI add-on. To learn more, please check the documentation .

items.title: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications adds support for smart card redirection
items.description: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications now supports smart card redirection on single-session and multi-session fleets, so users can access the smart card connected to their local device from applications inside their streaming session. It also extends smart card sign-in, previously limited to single-session fleets, to multi-session fleets. This launch helps public sector, healthcare, and other regulated organizations that use Common Access Card (CAC) or Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards run those workflows on multi-session fleets. Administrators can turn smart card sign-in for Active Directory and smart card redirection on or off independently for each stack. Smart card sign-in lets users sign in to domain-joined streaming instances with their smart card instead of a password, while redirected smart cards support in-session authentication, digital signing, and email encryption. For example, a government agency can move CAC users from single-session to multi-session fleets and keep CAC sign-in. These capabilities are available today in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) regions that offer WorkSpaces Applications. To get started, turn on either setting under User settings for your stack, use a Windows image with the latest WorkSpaces Applications agent, and connect with the WorkSpaces Applications client for Windows. New stacks have both settings turned off by default, and existing stacks that use smart card redirection keep it turned on. To learn more, see Create a stack in the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications Administration Guide, or visit the Amazon WorkSpaces Applications product page.

items.title: Amazon EMR Serverless introduces Flex execution
items.description: Amazon EMR Serverless now supports Flex execution, a new option that reduces the cost of non-urgent Spark batch jobs by up to 60% by running them on spare compute capacity. With Flex, you enable a single configuration when submitting a job, with no changes to Spark scripts or job definitions. Flex execution is designed for workloads that have flexible completion requirements, such as nightly batch ETL, backfill jobs, and development or testing pipelines. Start and execution times of Flex jobs vary because spare compute resources may not always be available immediately and may be reclaimed during execution. To reduce the likelihood and impact of interruptions, EMR Serverless spans availability zones, diversifies across instance types, places the Spark driver on dedicated capacity to protect job state, and retries interrupted tasks through Spark's built-in fault tolerance. You can also use Flex execution with Serverless Storage to offload shuffle data, adding another layer of resilience where retried tasks can resume from stored intermediate results instead of recomputing previous stages. Regardless of the execution option, Spark jobs on EMR Serverless have the same capabilities, including AWS Lake Formation fine-grained access control, AWS Graviton-based workers, and AWS Glue Data Catalog integration. Flex workers are billed at Flex rates for vCPU-hours and memory GB-hours, while the Spark driver and storage are billed at Standard rates. Amazon EMR Serverless Flex execution is available on all EMR releases and in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR Serverless is available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, except the China Regions. To learn more, see Flex execution in the Amazon EMR Serverless User Guide and the blog post - Introducing Amazon EMR Serverless Flex . For pricing details, visit the Amazon EMR pricing page .

items.title: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available
items.description: Amazon EMR 8.2 is now available with new features across Amazon EMR on EC2, Amazon EMR on EKS, and Amazon EMR Serverless. This release upgrades Apache Spark to 4.1.3, Apache Iceberg to 1.11.0, and Delta Lake to 4.2.0, and it is designated a Long Term Support (LTS) release. This release makes it easier to run secure, governed analytics at scale - you can now write to the same Delta Lake table on Amazon S3 from multiple clusters concurrently, refresh Iceberg materialized views incrementally, and propagate end-user identity from Spark jobs and interactive sessions all the way to AWS Lake Formation and Amazon S3 so access is authorized and audited as the original user. Amazon EMR 8.2 expands governance and performance across all three deployment options. New features include concurrent Delta Lake writes using Amazon S3 conditional writes (no DynamoDB log store required), and Lake Formation fine-grained access control (FGAC) now covers materialized views, governed user-defined functions, more Iceberg operations, and a broader set of Spark SQL features. The release also adds OpenLineage-based lineage capture to the AWS Glue Data Catalog and trusted identity propagation for steps and sessions. With EMR 8.2, data engineers can now precompute each pipeline stage as an Iceberg materialized view in SQL. Each materialized view refreshes only the changes instead of recomputing the entire source table across projections, inner joins, filters and SUM, COUNT aggregations. Specific to EMR on EC2, this release adds Spark Connect support on multi-primary clusters, along with Secret Agent improvements that cut user-provisioning latency by up to 97% under high concurrency. On EMR Serverless, new scaling profiles for Spark (performance-optimized, balanced, or cost-optimized) let you tune how quickly executors scale, and applications can now run Lake Formation-governed Glue UDFs. On EMR on EKS, the Spark Operator is upgraded to version 2 (based on open-source Spark Operator 2.5.0). Amazon EMR 8.2 is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR is available. To learn more, see the Amazon EMR 8.2 Release Guide for EMR on EC2, the EMR Serverless release notes , and the EMR on EKS release notes , or get started by creating a cluster from the Amazon EMR console .

items.title: Introducing the Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless
items.description: Amazon EMR Serverless now offers the Apache Spark optimization agent, which analyzes completed Spark job runs and delivers cost and performance optimization recommendations in seconds. You can select a cost or performance goal, and the agent returns specific configuration changes with the telemetry evidence and plain-language reasoning behind each suggestion. The agent can analyze a single run or compare it against a known-good baseline to pinpoint what changed. You access it from the EMR Serverless console or through the SageMaker Unified Studio MCP Server. The agent takes the job's configuration, logs, and Spark telemetry together with your chosen intent and returns recommendations computed by a deterministic recommendation engine. The engine reads all job artifacts together to identify what is driving runtime and cost: too little parallelism, a skewed join key, memory pressure forcing spill, idle executors, or capacity provisioned beyond what the job uses. The configurations the engine targets are the settings most commonly tuned across millions of Spark jobs running on AWS. When cost and performance trade off, the recommendation improves the metric you asked for while keeping degradation of the other within defined limits. The engine also evaluates a best practices checklist covering platform-level improvements such as upgrading to a newer Spark version or using Graviton processors. Each recommendation is labeled by the surface it modifies: infrastructure, Spark configuration, code, or data layout. Data engineers can also use the agent during development to tune configurations before promoting to production. All access is authenticated with AWS IAM and logged in AWS CloudTrail. The Apache Spark Optimization Agent is available at no additional charge in all Regions where EMR Serverless is available, except GovCloud (US) and China Regions, for EMR release versions 7.6 and later. To get started, see Apache Spark Optimization Agent for Amazon EMR Serverless .

items.title: AWS Transform now accelerates migration deals for Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) benefits
items.description: AWS Partners can now expedite Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) deals, from qualification to incentive payout, with an end-to-end agentic workflow in AWS Transform. Partners can manage the full MAP lifecycle without leaving AWS Transform, including deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, migration planning and execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement. Previously, Partners had to switch between separate systems for opportunity discovery, assessments, deal qualification, funding approvals, agreement execution, resource tagging, and incentive disbursement. This fragmentation, along with manual handoffs between steps, led to longer qualification cycles. Now, with the agentic MAP experience in AWS Transform, Partners connect their AWS Partner Central account and invite customers into the same engagement. Partners start by scoping customer environments with the built-in agentic discovery tool, or by importing data from RVTools or AWS-validated ISV tools listed in AWS Marketplace. AWS Transform then combines this discovery data with opportunity details from APN Customer Engagements (ACE) to automatically qualify Partner-initiated opportunities in a guided flow, so Partners get eligibility decisions sooner and close deals faster. As the migration progresses, MAP resource tags are applied automatically, and Partner cash and customer credits are disbursed based on actual usage data. Throughout, customers get shared, real-time visibility into migration projects alongside their Partner. AWS Transform with integrated MAP is now available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is supported . To learn more, visit the AWS Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) page. Partners can get started with the AWS Partner Central user guide (login required) or by contacting their Partner Development Manager. Customers can contact their AWS account team or AWS Partner.

items.title: Amazon EC2 C8gn instances are now available in AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region
items.description: Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8gn instances, powered by the latest-generation AWS Graviton4 processors, are available in the AWS Israel (Tel Aviv) region. The C8gn instances provide up to 30% better compute performance than Graviton3-based Amazon EC2 C7gn instances. Amazon EC2 C8gn instances feature the latest 6th generation AWS Nitro Cards, and offer up to 600 Gbps network bandwidth, the highest network bandwidth among network optimized EC2 instances.  Take advantage of the enhanced networking capabilities of C8gn to scale performance and throughput, while optimizing the cost of running network-intensive workloads such as network virtual appliances, data analytics, CPU-based artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) inference.  For increased scalability, C8gn instances offer instance sizes up to 48xlarge, up to 384 GiB of memory, and up to 120 Gbps of bandwidth to Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS). C8gn instances support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking on the 16xlarge, 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl sizes, which enables lower latency and improved cluster performance for workloads deployed on tightly coupled clusters.  C8gn instances are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon, N.California), Europe (Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London, Spain, Zurich, Milan, Paris), Asia Pacific (Singapore, Malaysia, Sydney, Thailand, Mumbai, Seoul, Melbourne, Jakarta, Hyderabad, Tokyo, Hong Kong), Middle East (UAE), Israel (Tel Aviv), Africa (Cape Town), Canada West (Calgary, Central), South America (Sao Paulo), AWS GovCloud (US-East, US-West).   To learn more, see Amazon C8gn Instances . To begin your Graviton journey, visit the Level up your compute with AWS Graviton page . To get started, see AWS Management Console , AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , and AWS SDKs .

items.title: Amazon EC2 C8ine instances are now available in AWS Europe (Ireland) region
items.description: Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8ine instances are available in the AWS Europe (Ireland) region. C8ine instances are powered by custom sixth generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors, available only on AWS. These instances feature the latest sixth generation AWS Nitro cards, delivering up to 43% higher performance compared to previous generation C6in instances. C8ine instances offer up to 2.5 times higher packet performance per vCPU versus prior generation network optimized instances, providing up to 2x higher network throughput for traffic going through Internet gateways compared to existing C6in network optimized instances. C8ine instances are designed for security and network virtual appliances, including virtual firewalls, load balancers, and Telco 5G UPF workloads. Amazon EC2 C8ine instances are available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland, Frankfurt) regions. C8ine instances are available via Savings Plans, On-Demand, and Spot instances. For more information, visit the Amazon EC2 C8i instance pages.

items.title: Amazon ECR now supports global authentication tokens for private registries
items.description: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports global authentication tokens for private registries. Previously, you needed to request a separate authentication token in each AWS Region where you push or pull container images. Now, you can request a single token from the AWS Sign-In CreateBearerToken API and use it across all ECR private registries in the same AWS partition. Teams that run proxy services to route container pulls across Regions, a common pattern for optimizing latency or availability, previously had to request, refresh, and coordinate a separate token for every Region behind the proxy. With global tokens, the proxy manages one token for all Regions in the AWS partition. Global tokens are valid for 12 hours by default, but can be configured to be as low as 5 minutes. These tokens work with the Docker CLI, and the Amazon ECR Docker Credential Helper. Existing regional authentication tokens continue to work as before. Global authentication tokens are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is supported. To learn more, see Private registry authentication in the Amazon ECR User Guide .

items.title: Customize AWS Elemental Inference with custom models, prompts, and decisions
items.description: AWS Elemental Inference now lets you customize how it analyzes your live video in two ways. You can create functions that ask custom questions of the video using multi-modal foundational models in Amazon Bedrock, or add contextual metadata decisions using labels and questions you define. Both run on the same pipeline as built-in features such as vertical video creation and smart subtitles, and return results through the GetMetadata API, with no separate pipeline to build. Use contextual metadata decisions when the answer you need fits labels and yes/no questions. You define yes/no questions, such as whether a scene is a weather report, or "pick-one" categories, such as genre. For each scene, contextual metadata returns a decision and a confidence score for every label and question, alongside the standard Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM), and mood fields, so your workflows can act when confidence meets a threshold you set. No model selection or prompt writing is required. Use functions for open-ended answers, custom response formats, or analysis contextual metadata doesn't cover, such as sponsor logo exposure. A function specifies an Amazon Bedrock model and JSONata expressions that shape the request and response. You attach it to a feed and choose how frequently it runs. Contextual-metadata decisions configuration is included in the contextual metadata price. Functions are available at no additional charge on feeds with at least one feature active; Amazon Bedrock usage is billed separately. Both are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental Inference is available. To learn more, see the AWS Elemental Inference user guide .

items.title: AWS Security Hub now infers resource criticality from installed software and usage
items.description: Today, AWS Security Hub adds installed software and resource usage as signals for resource criticality, which indicates how important a resource is to your business. Security Hub uses criticality to rank exposure findings, so that central security teams can prioritize the exposures that affect their most important resources. Security Hub already infers criticality from resource tags and names, but inconsistently tagged resources often have an Unknown criticality, which makes their exposures harder to prioritize. With installed software and resource usage as additional signals, more of your resources receive a meaningful criticality with no tagging or configuration required. For example, an EC2 instance that runs a database engine and serves steady traffic receives a higher criticality than an instance that runs only monitoring agents and sits idle. These signals are included with the Security Hub Essentials plan at no additional cost and require no new enablement. To learn more, see Resources in Security Hub in the AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page . For a list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available, see the AWS Region table .
